The Karnataka Milk Federation is the apex body of Karnataka's dairy co-operatives and the home of the Nandini brand. KMF recruitment is announced only through official notifications. Check this page and the official notification PDF.

Any application fee is paid only in the way the official notification describes.

Frequently asked questions
› How do I apply?
Open the official notification (PDF) and read it fully. If applications are online, the "Apply" button takes you to the official application site. Follow the steps, fees and documents listed in the notification.
› Am I eligible?
Eligibility (qualification, age limit, reservation and experience) is different for every post and is given in its notification. Check it carefully before applying.
› Where will results and admit cards appear?
In the "Results, admit cards & updates" section of this page, next to the recruitment they belong to, and through any other channel stated in the notification.
› Do district milk unions recruit separately?
District milk unions are separate co-operative bodies and may run their own recruitment. Always check which organisation is recruiting in the official notification.
› Does KMF charge money for jobs?
No. KMF never sells jobs or collects money through personal accounts. Treat any such request as fraud (see the warning on this page).

HISTORY OF MILK
HISTORY OF MILK
The history of milk is a fascinating journey that intertwines with the evolution of human civilization and the domestication of animals. As early humans transitioned from a nomadic lifestyle to settled agricultural communities, the realization that certain animals could provide a steady supply of milk marked a pivotal moment. The domestication of animals like cows, goats, and sheep was a transformative development.
Humans first learned to consume the milk of other mammals regularly following the domestication of animals during the Neolithic Revolution or the development of agriculture. This development occurred independently in several global locations from as early as 9000–7000 BC in Mesopotamia.
The history of dairy in the Indian subcontinent goes back roughly 8,000 years to the first domestication of zebu cattle, which is thought to have originated in India. By the beginning of the Indus Valley civilisation (c. 3300 – c. 1300 BCE), zebu cattle had been fully domesticated and used for their milk. Sheep and Goats were also domesticated.

docs.title: History of Milk
docs.text:
In the Vedic period (c. 1500 – c. 500 BCE), milk was one of the primary elements of the typical diet. Milk and milk products including clarified butter were consumed. Yogurt (curd) was another form in which milk was consumed during the period. The Vedas describe curdling of milk by mixing a portion of soured milk into it. They also mention curdling of milk by the addition of plant substances such as the bark of the palash tree and the fruit of jujube, which may have contained rennet-like enzymes. These are some of the earliest documented references to enzymatic cheese-making.
According to the Sutra literature, during the period c. 800 – c. 300 BCE, boiled rice with milk or curd continued to be a common food item. Cows used to be milked twice a day. The ones which were pregnant or undergoing their estrous cycle or nursing a calf of another cow were not milked. The preparation of payasa is also noted. Madhuparka – a mixture of honey with curds or ghee was used for welcoming guests. The preparation of a sweet with clarified butter as one of the ingredients is also mentioned.

our-journeys
Karnataka Milk Federation – a harbinger of rural prosperity
Karnataka Milk Federation (KMF) is the largest cooperative dairy Federation in South India, owned and managed by milk producers of Karnataka State. KMF has over 2 million milk producers in over 16149 Dairy Cooperative Societies at village level, functioning under 16 District Cooperative Milk Unions in Karnataka State. The mission of the federation is to usher rural prosperity through dairy development. During the last four decades of cooperative dairy development by KMF, the dairy industry in Karnataka has progressed from a situation of milk-scarcity to that of milk-surplus.
“Quality Excellence from Cow to Consumer” is the motto of the Federation to obtain better-quality Milk and milk products from our value chain (Procurement to Processing to Marketing). Thus milk and milk products under the “Nandini” brand name are unmatched in quality and available to consumers at competitive prices. In a way Nandini Milk and Milk Products are “Spreading wealth of health”.
Karnataka Cooperative Milk Producers Federation Limited (KMF) is the Apex Body in Karnataka representing Dairy Farmers Co-operatives.

docs.title: our-journeys
docs.text:
It is the second largest dairy co-operative in the country and the largest in South India in procurement and sales. One of the core functions of the Federation is marketing of Milk and Milk Products. Nandini is a household name for pure and fresh milk and milk products.
KMF has 16 Milk Unions throughout the State, which procure milk from Primary Dairy Cooperative Societies (DCS) and distribute milk to consumers in towns, cities and rural markets of Karnataka.
The first ever World Bank funded Dairy Development Program in the country started in Karnataka with the organization of Village Level Dairy Co-operatives in 1974. The AMUL/ANAND pattern of dairy cooperatives started functioning in Karnataka from 1974–75 with financial assistance from World Bank under Operation Flood II & III. Dairy cooperatives were structured in three tiers — Village Level Dairy Co-operatives at the base, District Milk Unions at the middle level handling procurement, processing and marketing, and the Karnataka Milk Federation at the Apex level coordinating the statewide activities.
Coordination of activities among the Unions and developing the market for Milk and Milk products is the responsibility of KMF.

docs.text:
Milk marketing is organized by respective Unions within their jurisdiction. Surplus/deficit milk among unions is balanced by KMF. All milk and milk products within and outside the State are marketed by KMF under the “NANDINI” brand.
Objectives
KMF is a Cooperative Apex Body in Karnataka implementing all-round dairy development activities to achieve the following:
• Ensure assured and remunerative market for milk produced by farmer members.
• Provide quality milk and dairy products to urban consumers.
• Build and develop village-level cooperative institutions to manage dairy activities.
• Provide inputs for milk production, processing, and dissemination of know-how.
• Facilitate rural development by providing self-employment opportunities, preventing migration, introducing cash economy, and creating sustained income.
The philosophy of dairy development is to eliminate middlemen and organize institutions owned and managed by milk producers with professional support.

docs.title: our-journeys
docs.text:
The core objective is achieving economies of scale to ensure maximum returns to producers while providing wholesome milk to consumers at reasonable prices.
Ultimately, this cooperative network bridges rural producers and urban consumers, bringing socio-economic development across Karnataka.
Evolution
Karnataka Milk Federation (KMF) evolved as a premier and profitable dairy farmers’ organization in Karnataka. In 1975, Karnataka Dairy Development Corporation (KDDC) was formed to implement World Bank Aided Dairy Projects. As dairying spread across the State, KMF emerged in 1983 covering the entire State with 13 District Milk Unions that performed activities including: organizing Dairy Co-operatives, Milk Routes, Veterinary Services, two-shift milk procurement, chilling, processing, distribution, and establishment of Cattle Feed Plants, Nandini Sperm Station, Liquid Nitrogen Supply and Training Centers.
The structure was modeled after the ANAND pattern dairy cooperatives.

docs.title: our-journeys
docs.text:
Initially, eight southern districts were targeted for organizing 1800 Dairy Co-operatives, four Milk Unions and processing facilities of 6.5 lakh liters/day by 1984.
Under Operation Flood II & III (1984 & 1987), the rest of Karnataka was covered. Thirteen unions were organized in 175 talukas of 20 districts. Processing facilities like chilling centers, dairies and powder plants were gradually transferred to District Unions. Additional facilities were added every decade with support from Govt., Zilla Panchayat, and NDDB. Today the processing capacity is 32.25 lakh liters/day and continues to expand.
Company Objectives
Karnataka Milk Federation (KMF) aims to:
• Provide assured and remunerative market for milk from farmer members.
• Provide quality milk to urban consumers.
• Build village-level cooperative institutions to manage dairy operations.
• Facilitate rural development through self-employment, reduced migration, cash economy and steady income.
The philosophy focuses on eliminating middlemen and empowering producers through cooperative ownership and professional management.

food-safety
During the last ten years, the Federation is giving greater emphasis on procuring quality milk from DCSs under the concept of “Quality Excellence from Cow to Consumer.” Many Clean Milk Production (CMP) initiatives have been implemented at all the stages of procurement, processing and marketing. Among these CMP initiatives, noteworthy initiative is the setting up of Community Milking Parlours in villages.
The KMF is forerunner to introduce this innovative technological initiative for bringing about revolutionary improvement in quality of milk collected in DCSs. This system has several advantages such as elimination of mastitis in milch animals and improvement of productivity. The milk from milking machines, collected through Automatic Computerized Milk Collection Units is chilled directly in Bulk Milk Coolers. This chilled raw milk, untouched and unadulterated by human hands, has very high microbiological quality, comparable to international standards.

Animal Breeding
Animal Breeding
Our breeding program focuses on improving the genetic potential of cattle by introducing scientifically proven breeding techniques and high-quality semen.
Program Highlights:
Artificial Insemination (AI) services at village and district levels
Use of genetically superior bulls for breed enhancement
Pregnancy diagnosis and reproductive health monitoring
Promotion of high-yielding crossbreeds and indigenous breed improvement
Calf management guidance for better future productivity
Record keeping for AI, calving, and breeding cycles
Objective:
To enhance the genetic quality of dairy animals, improve fertility, and increase milk production sustainably.

Animal Health
Animal health services are essential to maintaining high milk yield and ensuring the wellbeing of livestock. The cooperative provides accessible and professional veterinary care at the village and taluk levels

Regular health check-ups and routine treatments
Vaccination drives (FMD, HS, BQ, etc.)
Deworming and parasite control programs
Emergency veterinary support and first-aid services

Objective:

docs.title: Fodder Activities

Fodder Activities
Nutrition plays a crucial role in the productivity and health of dairy animals. The cooperative supports farmers in cultivating and accessing balanced and affordable cattle feed.
Fodder Initiatives:
Supply of high-quality fodder seeds and slips
Promotion of green fodder cultivation and fodder banks
Demonstration plots for fodder varieties
Training on ration balancing and low-cost feed management
Support for silage making and fodder conservation
Distribution of mineral mixtures and feed supplements
Objective:
To ensure year-round availability of nutritious fodder, reducing feed costs and improving milk yield for member farmers.

docs.title: Procurement
docs.text:
Procurement
The Dairy Cooperative ensures transparent and efficient milk procurement from farmers across all affiliated societies. Our procurement system is designed to support rural dairy farmers, encourage fair pricing, and maintain the highest standards of milk quality.
Key Activities:
Daily milk collection from village-level societies
Quality testing for fat, SNF, adulteration, and freshness
Immediate digital recording of milk quantity and quality
Timely payment to farmers through cooperative systems
Cold chain support to maintain milk freshness from farm to plant
Farmer awareness programs on hygienic milking and milk handling
Objective:
To create a reliable procurement ecosystem that guarantees farmers a stable income while ensuring high-quality milk supply to processing units.

1. Ksheera Bhagya:
• The Ksheera Bhagya Scheme was launched on 1st Aug 2013 by the Government of Karnataka in coordination with KMF to provide nutritious milk to School and Anganwadi children for healthy growth and development.
• It was a dream project conceived by KMF based on the suggestion of the Honorable Chief Minister of Karnataka to help poor children and also support milk producers by utilizing surplus milk.
2. Amruth Yojane:
The scheme was introduced in the 2007–08 budget to support socio-economic upliftment of Devadasis, widows, SC and ST women by providing a milch animal. The initial cost was Rs.20,000 (2007–08 to 2009–10), later increased to Rs.35,000.

Bengaluru: In a significant step towards sustainability, Karnataka Milk Federation (KMF) is set to introduce eco-friendly milk packaging for its popular brand, Nandini, in Bengaluru.
The new biodegradable milk packets are made from corn starch, sugarcane and other plant-based materials. Unlike conventional polythene packets that take over 500 years to decompose, these eco-friendly alternatives break down naturally within 90 days and can even be converted into organic fertiliser.
So far, the feedback has been very positive. No leakage, no compromise on milk quality, and high consumer satisfaction," said KMF managing director Shivaswamy B.
According to KMF officials, the biodegradable sachets look and feel similar to traditional plastic packaging, offering familiarity to consumers while being significantly more environmentally friendly. 
Raghunandan M, director of marketing at KMF, highlighted the broader impact of the switch. "We currently use 20 to 25 lakh plastic milk packets daily.

docs.title: Eco-Friendly Nandini Milk Packets Launch

Under the central govt's extended producer responsibility (EPR) policy, we spend heavily on recycling nearly 15,000 metric tonnes of plastic per year. Transitioning to biodegradable packaging will not only reduce this cost but also help us tackle Bengaluru's growing plastic waste problem.
Encouraged by the success of the pilot, KMF plans to roll out biodegradable milk packets across all Nandini outlets in Bengaluru from July. A statewide implementation is expected to follow soon after. 
If adopted widely, this initiative could set a new benchmark for sustainable dairy practices in India and significantly reduce the environmental impact of plastic waste in urban areas.

Not just the staple products, but ice creams have also seen an uptick in sales with a 40% increase from last year, the highest ever for KMF.

MK Jagadish, Managing Director of KMF, told TNIE that heat is one of the reasons, while during April — particularly between April 9 and 15 — festivals such as Ugadi, Ram Navami and Eid-ul-Fitr came one after the other. “This time, we have made improvements in the curd culture and are seeing that curd packets are flying off the shelf immediately. Usually, the cooperative supplies products twice a day. But given the demand in some areas, products have been supplied thrice,” Jagadish said.

KMF has made several supply-chain improvements given the increasing temperatures and ramped up the functioning and maintenance of cold storages in the state, he said.

But this year, the sales spiked to 48 lakh litres in a day. Similar was the case with curd and buttermilk. In the first week, we recorded 11.5 lakh litres and within five days, the number rose to 16.5 lakh litres, making Nandini a preferred brand,” he said.
KMF saw its highest-ever ice cream sales. “The ice cream sales are up by 40% and constantly improving. In February, we anticipated a hot summer in the state, so we wanted to be prepared with sufficient supply. Ice creams have a shelf-life of over a year. We decided to start production early. Nandini Milk Products
Nandini Milk Products
To meet the ever growing demand for milk based sweets, KMF has set up Nandini Milk Products Unit.
Nandini Milk Products is a specialized manufacturing unit of the Karnataka Milk Federation (KMF) established to cater to the growing national demand for traditional milk-based sweets and value-added dairy foods. The unit plays a crucial role in preserving and standardizing ethnic Indian dairy products while ensuring consistent quality, hygiene, and shelf life. It produces a wide range of popular sweets including Mysore Pak, Peda, Khova, Badam Burfi, Cashew Burfi, Coconut Burfi, Chocolate Burfi, and dry fruit-based varieties. In addition to traditional sweets, the unit also manufactures ready-to-eat products such as Khova Jamoon, Rosogolla, Jamoon Mix, Nandini Bite, and Badam Powder. Advanced processing technology, automated cooking systems, and strict quality control protocols are employed to meet food safety standards prescribed by FSSAI and ISO norms. Raw milk and inputs are sourced directly from KMF member unions, ensuring traceability and freshness.

Nandini Packaging Film Plant
KMF established Nandini Packaging Film Plant at Munnekolala, Bengaluru in 1998.
The Nandini Packaging Film Plant was established by Karnataka Milk Federation on 1st January 1998 at Munnekolala, Marathahalli, Bengaluru, on 4.5 acres of its own land. The plant was set up to meet KMF’s large and growing internal demand for flexible packaging films used for milk and milk products. Currently, KMF requires nearly 950 to 1000 metric tonnes of packaging film annually, and this unit plays a strategic role in ensuring uninterrupted supply. The plant manufactures multi-layer polyethylene films suitable for liquid milk pouches and other dairy packaging applications, conforming to food-grade safety standards. By having its own packaging unit, KMF has significantly reduced dependency on external suppliers, improved cost efficiency, and ensured consistent packaging quality across all unions. The facility is equipped with modern blown film extrusion technology and quality testing laboratories to maintain thickness, strength, and hygiene standards.

Dempo Dairy Limited
Dempo Dairy Industries Limited was taken over by KMF in 1993.
Dempo Dairy Industries Limited, located at Aasangi in Vijayapura district, was originally a private dairy unit that became financially sick and was placed under the Board for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR). Recognizing its strategic importance, Karnataka Milk Federation took over the unit in 1993 and successfully revived its operations. Post takeover, KMF invested in modernization, capacity enhancement, and quality systems, transforming the plant into a reliable dairy processing unit. Today, Dempo Dairy is an ISO-certified facility engaged in the production of skimmed milk powder, whole milk powder, butter, and other dairy ingredients. The unit primarily handles surplus milk procured during flush seasons, converting it into long-shelf-life products that help balance seasonal fluctuations. This conversion capability is critical to protecting farmer interests by preventing distress sales of milk. Dempo Dairy also contributes to KMF’s institutional and export supply requirements.

The Union adopted the “AMUL Pattern” for organizing milk cooperatives with the objective of socio-economic transformation of rural farmers by promoting dairying as a major subsidiary occupation.
Mysore Dairy, with an initial capacity of 10 TLPD, was started in 1965 under the Department of Animal Husbandry and Veterinary Services, Government of Karnataka. The dairy was transferred to Karnataka Dairy Development Corporation in 1974. Its capacity was expanded to 60 TLPD in 1980 and subsequently transferred to Karnataka Milk Federation in 1984. Tumakuru Co-operative Milk Union
Tumakuru Co-operative Milk Union
Tumkur Co-operative Milk Producers’ Societies Union Limited (TUMUL) is the district apex body for dairy development in Karnataka.
Area of Operation:
The area of operation covers the entire Tumkur district, comprising 10 taluks with a total of 2,977 revenue villages.
Tumkur Co-operative Milk Union has been certified with ISO 22000:2005 by DNV (Business Assurance – Food Safety System Certification) and is currently under the process of upgrading to ISO 22000:2018 certification from Bureau Veritas.
The Union was established under the World Bank project in 1975 and registered under the Co-operative Act on 30th March 1977, covering the entire Tumkur district as its operational area. Dairy development activities began in 1976 through the Karnataka Dairy Development Corporation (KDDC) with the objective of supporting milk marketing in the Bengaluru market. Initially, a 30,000-litre capacity farm cooler was established, which was later converted into a 60 TLPD feeder plant in 1981.
The processing capacity of the dairy was increased to 1.00 lakh litres per day in 2005 under the Perspective Plan – Phase I.

docs.title: Tumakuru Co-operative Milk Union
docs.text:
Due to rapid growth in milk procurement, the capacity was further enhanced to 3.25 lakh litres per day. A new packing block with increased capacity was inaugurated on 16-09-2013, followed by the inauguration of a new flexi milk packing block on 06-10-2016.
Membership and Share Amount:
As of the end of November 2024, the Union has 1,398 registered Dairy Co-operative Societies (DCS), out of which 1,389 are commissioned and 1,354 are functional. The total membership stands at 2,72,710, including 89,584 women members.
Milk Procurement:
During 1975–76, the average milk procurement was 1,035 kilograms per day. At the time of registration of the Union, procurement increased to 9,486 kilograms per day. Since then, milk procurement has grown multifold due to effective implementation of various input and support activities.
During the year 2024–25 (as of November 2024), the average milk procurement stands at 8.82 lakh kilograms per day. On 28-06-2024, the Union recorded its highest-ever procurement of 9.81 lakh kilograms per day since inception.
Milk Price:
The cost per kilogram of milk is calculated based on Fat and SNF content. The basic price is fixed for 4.0% Fat and 8.5% SNF.

docs.title: Tumakuru Co-operative Milk Union
docs.text:

A quality incentive of 30 paise per kg of milk is paid once a month if milk with SNF ≥ 8.5% constitutes more than 85% of the total milk procured.
Processing Capacity:
Tumkur Dairy was established in 1981 with a processing capacity of 60,000 litres per day. In 2005, under the Perspective Plan, the capacity was increased to 1.00 lakh litres per day.
At present, the dairy processes, packs and sells about 3.35 lakh litres of milk per day in Tumkur district and parts of Bengaluru urban and rural districts. In addition to liquid milk, the dairy produces curd, masala buttermilk, peda, Mysore pak, cashew burfi and ghee.
The Union operates four chilling centres located at Yediyur (60 TLPD), Sira (30 TLPD), K.B. Cross (60 TLPD) and Madhugiri (60 TLPD). Milk procurement and sales have exceeded expectations over the past few years.

The marketing area includes the entire Tumkur district and parts of Bengaluru urban and rural districts.

Hassan district, renowned for the exquisite Hoysala sculpture art, is home to world-famous heritage sites such as Belur, Halebidu and the Sravanabelagola monolithic statue built during the Ganga period. Belagavi Co-operative Milk Union
Belgaum district, popularly known as the sugar district, is located in the north-western part of Karnataka state, bounded by Goa state in the west and Maharashtra state in the north. The total area of the district is 13415 square kilometers and has 1138 villages. Krishna, Ghataprabha, Malaprabha, Vedaganga and Dudhganga are the major rivers of the district. Average rainfall in the district is 594.90 mm.
As the land here is fertile and there is naturally abundant green fodder available, and the climate of the district is suitable for dairy farming, the farmers rely on dairy farming as the main sub-crop along with agriculture. The number of dairy cows will be 7 lakhs as farmers are giving preference to rearing more dairy cows. The annual income of the district is Rs. 875.00 crores from dairy farming and related activities. As the district is irrigated and rainfed, sugarcane, tobacco, cotton are grown as cash crops, and paddy, cowpea, maize, oilseeds as food crops.

Dakshinna Kannada Co-operative Milk Union
Dakshina Kannada Milk Union was registered in the year 1986 under the Karnataka Co-operative Societies Act. The Union has jurisdiction over the twin districts of Dakshina Kannada and Udupi. The Union operates dairies with a combined milk processing capacity of 2.5 LLPD in both districts and has 749 functional Primary Milk Cooperative Societies (MPCS), including 200 women societies.
At the time of inception, the Union had an initial milk procurement of 4,500 kg per day. Over the years, procurement has steadily increased and currently stands at 4.85 lakh kg per day. The Union ensures high-quality milk collection at the MPCS level by providing Automatic Milk Collection Units (AMCUs), FATOMATIC machines, and Milk Analysers. Regular testing of milk is carried out for all farmers, resulting in improved milk quality. Farmer payments are made through Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT). The Union is also the only one supporting a dedicated calf-rearing scheme.
A unique feature of the Union is that milk from all societies is collected exclusively through Bulk Milk Coolers (BMCs).

docs.text:

The Union records milk sales of approximately 3.76 LLPD and curd sales of about 70,000 kg per day. Nearly 98% of Nandini milk is sold directly to customers. A strong dealer network of 1,784 active dealers supports distribution, with 1,024 dealers in Dakshina Kannada and 760 in Udupi districts. The Union has captured nearly 98% of the milk and curd market in its operational area.
The Union is known for supplying best-quality hygienic milk and milk products under the trusted Nandini brand. Efficient logistics enable delivery of milk and products to dealers two to three times a day using 103 insulated vehicles.

Dakshina Kannada Milk Union is deeply rooted in the region’s rich cultural heritage, often referred to as “Deva Daivagala Nadu.” Numerous temples in the Union’s jurisdiction rely on Nandini Ghee for preparing prasadam due to its superior quality. Raichur, Ballari & Koppal Milk Union
The Raichur-Ballari-Koppal cooperative union covers one of Karnataka’s largest operational areas by geography, spanning semi-arid zones where dairy acts as a vital income source for farming households. Operating across district borders, the union manages long supply chains — coordinating village societies, chilling infrastructure and transport to central processing units. Because of the large distances and climatic stresses, the union emphasizes cold-chain investments and decentralized chilling to prevent spoilage and maintain quality. Farmer support is focused on fodder security, breed improvement and veterinary services to reduce mortality and enhance yields. The union’s strategic development includes increasing processing capacity for value-added products that can be transported economically to urban markets, thereby improving returns to producers. Its role is central to rural livelihoods in the northern districts and to sustaining a stable regional dairy supply for both local consumption and inter-district trade.
